lesson_scope: Solving line-curve intersection problems requiring two distinct intersection points (D > 0) or no intersection points (D < 0), setting up linear/quadratic inequalities in an unknown parameter (gradient m or intercept c/k).

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: solving linear parameter inequality for no intersection condition D < 0.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving D < 0 for no line-curve intersection.

hints: Equate line and curve: $x^2 + 5 = 2x + c \implies x^2 - 2x + (5 - c) = 0$.
For no intersection, set discriminant strictly negative: $D < 0$.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations and set to zero:
$$x^2 + 5 = 2x + c$$
$$x^2 - 2x + (5 - c) = 0$$

Apply the condition for no real intersection points ($D < 0$):
$$D = (-2)^2 - 4(1)(5 - c) < 0$$
$$4 - 20 + 4c < 0$$
$$4c - 16 < 0$$

Solve for the constant $c$:
$$4c < 16 \implies c < 4$$

ai_rubric.observable: Equates curve and line: $x^2 - 2x + (5 - c) = 0$ and sets $(-2)^2 - 4(1)(5 - c) < 0$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: solving linear parameter inequality for two distinct points of intersection D > 0.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving D > 0 for two distinct intersections.

hints: Equate line and curve: $x^2 - 2x + 10 = 4x + k \implies x^2 - 6x + (10 - k) = 0$.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations and collect all terms:
$$x^2 - 2x + 10 = 4x + k$$
$$x^2 - 6x + (10 - k) = 0$$

Set the discriminant strictly positive for two distinct intersections:
$$D = (-6)^2 - 4(1)(10 - k) > 0$$
$$36 - 40 + 4k > 0$$
$$4k - 4 > 0$$

Solve for $k$:
$$4k > 4 \implies k > 1$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: solving a quadratic inequality in gradient m for distinct intersections.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving m^2 - k^2 > 0 for exterior intervals.

hints: Factorise $(m - 6)(m + 6) > 0$ to get the exterior regions: $m < -6$ or $m > 6$.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations:
$$x^2 + 8 = mx - 1$$
$$x^2 - mx + 9 = 0$$

Set the discriminant strictly positive for two distinct intersection points:
$$D = (-m)^2 - 4(1)(9) > 0$$
$$m^2 - 36 > 0$$
$$(m - 6)(m + 6) > 0$$

State the disjoint solution intervals:
$$m < -6 \quad \text{or} \quad m > 6$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: solving a quadratic inequality in gradient m for no intersection.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving m^2 - k^2 < 0 for interior interval.

hints: Factorise $(m - 4)(m + 4) < 0$ to get the interior interval: $-4 < m < 4$.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations:
$$x^2 + 2 = mx - 2$$
$$x^2 - mx + 4 = 0$$

Set the discriminant strictly negative for no intersection:
$$D = (-m)^2 - 4(1)(4) < 0$$
$$m^2 - 16 < 0$$
$$(m - 4)(m + 4) < 0$$

State the bounded solution interval:
$$-4 < m < 4$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: no-intersection condition with an inverted parabola.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving D < 0 with negative leading term.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations and rearrange to positive leading coefficient:
$$-x^2 + 4x - 1 = -2x + c$$
$$x^2 - 6x + (1 + c) = 0$$

Apply the no-intersection condition $D < 0$:
$$D = (-6)^2 - 4(1)(1 + c) < 0$$
$$36 - 4 - 4c < 0$$
$$32 - 4c < 0$$

Solve for $c$:
$$4c > 32 \implies c > 8$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: distinct intersections with non-monic leading coefficient a = 3.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving D > 0 with leading coefficient a > 1.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations:
$$3x^2 + 1 = 6x + k$$
$$3x^2 - 6x + (1 - k) = 0$$

Apply the condition for two distinct real points of intersection ($D > 0$):
$$D = (-6)^2 - 4(3)(1 - k) > 0$$
$$36 - 12(1 - k) > 0$$
$$24 + 12k > 0$$

Solve for the constant $k$:
$$12k > -24 \implies k > -2$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: solving linear inequality in constant k for line not intersecting a curve.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires finding range of k for which line does not intersect curve.

hints: Equate the line and curve equations: $x^2 + 7 = 3x + k \implies x^2 - 3x + (7 - k) = 0$.
For no intersection, set the discriminant strictly less than zero: $D < 0$.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations and rearrange to standard quadratic form:
$$x^2 + 7 = 3x + k$$
$$x^2 - 3x + (7 - k) = 0$$

Apply the condition for no intersection ($D < 0$):
$$D = (-3)^2 - 4(1)(7 - k) < 0$$
$$9 - 28 + 4k < 0$$
$$4k - 19 < 0$$

Solve the linear inequality for $k$:
$$4k < 19 \implies k < \dfrac{19}{4} \quad (\text{or } k < 4.75)$$

ai_rubric.observable: Equates line and curve to get $x^2 - 3x + (7 - k) = 0$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: quadratic inequality in gradient m for two distinct intersections.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires finding range of gradient m for two distinct intersections.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations:
$$x^2 = mx - 4$$
$$x^2 - mx + 4 = 0$$

Apply the condition for two distinct real roots ($D > 0$):
$$D = (-m)^2 - 4(1)(4) > 0$$
$$m^2 - 16 > 0$$
$$(m - 4)(m + 4) > 0$$

State the solution set:
$$m < -4 \quad \text{or} \quad m > 4$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: formulating discriminant expression in c and solving for two distinct intersections.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires forming single quadratic equation and finding discriminant expression.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations:
$$2x^2 - 6x + 5 = 2x + c$$
$$2x^2 - 8x + (5 - c) = 0$$

Evaluate the discriminant $D = b^2 - 4ac$:
$$D = (-8)^2 - 4(2)(5 - c)$$
$$D = 64 - 40 + 8c = 24 + 8c$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires finding range of c for two distinct intersections.

hints: For two distinct points of intersection, require $D > 0$.

walkthrough.text:
For two distinct points of intersection, the discriminant must be strictly positive:
$$24 + 8c > 0$$

Solve for the constant $c$:
$$8c > -24 \implies c > -3$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: showing quadratic inequality in k from no-intersection condition and solving the three-part inequality.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires establishing quadratic inequality in k from no-intersection condition.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations:
$$x^2 + 4x + 7 = kx - 2$$
$$x^2 + (4 - k)x + 9 = 0$$

Apply the condition for no intersection ($D < 0$):
$$D = (4 - k)^2 - 4(1)(9) < 0$$
$$16 - 8k + k^2 - 36 < 0$$
$$k^2 - 8k - 20 < 0$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires solving quadratic inequality for parameter interval.

hints: The roots of the quadratic are $k = -2$ and $k = 10$.
Since the inequality is $< 0$, the solution is the interior region: $-2 < k < 10$.

walkthrough.text:
Factorise the quadratic inequality:
$$(k - 10)(k + 2) < 0$$
$$\text{Critical values: } k = -2 \quad \text{and} \quad k = 10$$

State the interior interval for $< 0$:
$$-2 < k < 10$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: finding tangent boundary and deducing no-intersection range for inverted parabola.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires finding parameter for tangency boundary.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and inverted parabola and rearrange to standard quadratic form:
$$-x^2 + 5x - 3 = x + k$$
$$x^2 - 4x + (3 + k) = 0$$

Set the discriminant to zero for tangency:
$$D = (-4)^2 - 4(1)(3 + k) = 0$$
$$16 - 12 - 4k = 0$$
$$4 - 4k = 0 \implies k = 1$$

ai_rubric.observable: Equates to $x^2 - 4x + (3 + k) = 0$ and sets $(-4)^2 - 4(3 + k) = 0$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires deducing no-intersection range from tangency boundary.

hints: Geometrically, increasing $k$ lifts the line above the maximum of the inverted curve.

walkthrough.text:
For the line not to intersect the curve, require $D < 0$:
$$4 - 4k < 0$$
$$4k > 4$$

State the resulting range for $k$:
$$k > 1$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: line and curve intersection yielding quadratic inequality with non-rational surd critical values.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires forming quadratic inequality in k and finding exact surd roots.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations:
$$x^2 + kx + 5 = 2x - k$$
$$x^2 + (k - 2)x + (5 + k) = 0$$

Apply the condition for two distinct intersections ($D > 0$):
$$D = (k - 2)^2 - 4(1)(5 + k) > 0$$
$$k^2 - 4k + 4 - 20 - 4k > 0$$
$$k^2 - 8k - 16 > 0$$

Find the exact critical values by quadratic formula or completing the square:
$$(k - 4)^2 - 32 = 0$$
$$k = 4 \pm \sqrt{32} = 4 \pm 4\sqrt{2}$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires stating disjoint exterior interval with exact surd boundaries.

hints: For $k^2 - 8k - 16 > 0$, the quadratic is strictly positive outside the roots.

walkthrough.text:
For a strictly positive quadratic inequality ($> 0$), choose the exterior regions:
$$k < 4 - 4\sqrt{2} \quad \text{or} \quad k > 4 + 4\sqrt{2}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies outside regions for strictly positive quadratic inequality.

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: two-parameter no-intersection condition proof, interval deduction, and geometric interpretation.

hints: Equate line and curve: $(p - 1)x^2 + 4x + 3 = mx + 2 \implies (p - 1)x^2 + (4 - m)x + 1 = 0$.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the line and curve equations:
$$(p - 1)x^2 + 4x + 3 = mx + 2$$
$$(p - 1)x^2 + (4 - m)x + 1 = 0$$

Apply the no-intersection condition $D < 0$:
$$D = (4 - m)^2 - 4(p - 1)(1) < 0$$
$$(4 - m)^2 < 4(p - 1)$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires evaluating parameter interval and interpreting midpoint gradient geometrically.

hints: When $m = 4$, $(m - 4)^2 = 0$, which gives the maximum separation below the curve (the midpoint of the non-intersecting gradient range).

walkthrough.text:
Substitute $p = 10$ into the inequality:
$$(m - 4)^2 < 4(10 - 1) = 36$$

Solve the double inequality for $m$:
$$-6 < m - 4 < 6$$
$$-2 < m < 10$$

Interpret the case $m = 4$:
$$\text{At } m = 4, (m - 4)^2 = 0 \text{ is minimized, so } D = -36 < 0 \text{ is maximally negative.}$$
$$\text{Geometrically, } m = 4 \text{ represents the central gradient of the non-intersecting envelope of lines.}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that $m = 4$ is the midpoint of the non-intersecting gradient interval.
